prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing neutral-atom clocks to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from IceCube (B043) to optical lattice clocks (B059), Katori and Ye. My reasons are scientific and about credit, not about counting. A lattice clock is a new measurement technique in the sense I value: magic-wavelength trapping removes Doppler, recoil and Stark shifts together, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once, and that is what took neutral-atom clocks to about 1e-18. The result has been reproduced and surpassed in independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE), comparisons between clocks are routine, and the consequences are physical: centimetre-scale redshift measurements, tests of constants and dark-matter searches. The interpretation is not in doubt and the systematics are well understood, which is exactly the maturity test I apply as an experimentalist. On the chair's own question about distinctness, my answer is that the 2005 prize gave the comb as clockwork and the 2012 prize gave control of single trapped ions, whereas the lattice clock solves a different problem, so the citation must rest on magic-wavelength trapping and the 1e-18 uncertainty and must not mention the comb or optical clocks in general. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori proposed the scheme and made the first demonstrations, and Ye's group took stability and systematic uncertainty to the frontier and used the clock as a many-body system.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap and priority. A sceptic can read the lattice clock as the best application of the already honoured comb and ion-control work, and Ye's own standing owes something to the comb. Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow and Takamoto have real contributions to the line, and the Katori and Ye boundary must be checked against the 2003 to 2006 primary record. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so the headline payoff is still pending. I also set aside my own first choice for reasons I should state plainly: B043 has an unsettled third name among the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND leaders, and individual source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are still at modest significance without independent confirmation by KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD at IceCube depth. I think those reservations are real but I accept that colleagues in my own field may weigh them less heavily than I now do.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B059 first as a new measurement technique with independent confirmation, and notes that Lemonde, Gill, Bloom and Ludlow need to be checked against the primary record, and that Ye's work builds partly on the comb.
responses.response: In round 1 I told you I would move B059 higher if the precedent showed the committee treating it as a distinct discovery. Your own framing, a technique that opened new physics, persuaded me, and the independent reproduction you list is the confirmation I ask of any result. On priority, I agree it must be settled before the vote and I suggest we ask an external reviewer for the 2003 to 2006 record. I would keep the citation limited to magic-wavelength trapping and 1e-18 uncertainty. Your disclosed link to the Hall lineage is a proximity, not a tie to the credited work, and I am content that you vote, but the committee should record it.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B059 first as precision atomic physics at its best, with theory and experiment in agreement, and does not regard Lemonde, Gill, Bloom and others as a reason for a third name.
responses.response: You are better placed than I am on the atomic physics, so I take your judgement seriously: the comb and ion-control prizes supplied tools and a different clock architecture, and the lattice clock addresses Doppler, recoil and Stark shifts together. That answers my round-1 doubt about distinctness. Where I would still ask for care is the one you and Johansson both raise, whether Ye's credit is for the lattice clock or partly for the earlier comb work. I think the citation can solve this by naming only the lattice clock and its uncertainty, and I would accept two names. If an outside reviewer finds a third claimant with a decisive role in 2003 to 2006 we should reopen it, and I would not add a name without that evidence.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the proposal and first strontium demonstrations are Katori's while Ye's decisive contribution is performance and many-body clock physics, and says the citation should reflect that boundary.
responses.response: I agree that this boundary decides the citation, and my draft wording attempts to respect it by crediting the invention and realisation of the lattice clock and its performance at 1e-18, which covers both of them. I would not split the prize into two parts for this reason, because the single achievement is shared and a split would invite a bigger priority argument. You also asked about a method prize alongside B059. I do not see a second part on the shortlist that I could defend on attribution, so I prefer a single part. Your move from aberration-corrected microscopy, given your disclosed conflict, was proper.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery first and lists IceCube second, arguing that the Higgs has the largest scale of consequence and a decade of confirmation, and that the attribution cost is acceptable.
responses.response: I agree about scale and I ranked B019 second myself, so my difference is again attribution, and my round-1 reasoning has not changed. The committee would be choosing among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee on leadership roles in two collaborations of thousands, and the rule that no more than three people be named leaves out a founder with the same standing as the others. You conceded that cost yourself. I cannot see a three-name set that I could defend to the Academy as a statement about scientific decisions, so B019 stays as an alternative, not as my preference. If the committee develops an agreed account of who made the decisive choices in the two detectors, I will listen.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, arguing that the phases are reproduced by independent groups and that the prize would be for the phases and not for the pairing mechanism.
responses.response: You answered my round-1 question directly and I accept that a prize for the correlated and superconducting phases does not need a settled mechanism. Reproduction by Dean's and Young's groups matters to me. My remaining difficulty is credit: Cao, Fatemi and the other first experimentalists are outside the three names, and in a field only eight years old I would feel safer waiting for the record to settle. This is a judgement in your field and I defer to you on the physics, but I do not move my vote to B034 now and I do not list it as an alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the primary record of 2003 to 2006 supports Katori and Ye alone, or whether Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow or Takamoto have a claim the committee would need to recognise. I have not verified this and am relying on the atomic-physics members and an outside reviewer.
Whether the lattice clock is a distinct achievement from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. This is outside my expertise and I am relying on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second is a sign of maturity or a reason to wait. I lean toward maturity but it is not decisive.
Whether my reassessment of B043 is too severe: the diffuse flux is secure, and a future prize might name different people once KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD confirm source associations.
I have not independently verified the collaboration histories cited in the discussion, which come from memory.
statement.conflict_note: I have no known connection to Katori, Ye, JILA, RIKEN or the other lattice-clock groups, and I work in astroparticle physics at KTH, so B059 is outside my field and I rely on colleagues for the atomic physics. I still flag that my expertise there is limited. I previously flagged proximity to the IceCube community through astroparticle physics, and since B043 is now an alternative I note that this proximity remains. As chair I note that my own first choice in the opening ballot and round 1 was B043 and that I have changed it.
